title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
text:
8        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

On March 8, 1891, the office of manager having become vacant by the removal from the city of Eldridge K. Norworthy, the club selected Robert F. Naylor as manager, and Henry Naylor as critic.

"East Lynne" was then chosen as a play to be given. Other plays selected were "The Assessor" and "The Sham Doctor". These were given in a public performance on May 14, 1891, with the purpose of "raising funds with which to purchase a bell for Savoy College." Tickets were 35 cents; general admission 25 cents, reserved seats 50 cents. Receipts were $26.75. Some of the plays were repeated the next night, at which time receipts were $18.50.

This appears to have been the last performance of the club and as its objectives—a bell and a belfry—had been achieved, its members met on May 25, 1891, and reluctantly disbanded.

S. H. N. & T. TELEGRAPH COMPANY

While not an activity of Savoy College itself, the formation, in 1888, of a telegraph company, organized by a large group of students of the school, linked its operations closely with the activities of the college. About twenty ambitious young men and women became students of the Morse system and gained proficiency therein, looking to telegraphy as a profession and means of livelihood with marked success. The group constructed a line from Savoy to Potts, meandering en route to touch the stations of its members, and ultimately extended the line an approximate of nine miles. The promoters were W. Tom Sprewls, L. W. (Tobe) Hughes, Eldridge K. Norworthy, Tom Sadusk[?], who was one of the first to drop out of the organization; then his successors were Tom C. Frank, general superintendent; E. K. Norworthy, superintendent division one (Tom); E. K. Rubitski, superintendent division two (Bobs); Miss Ursula Sprewls, commercial department among students of which: Lula Sprewls, William F. Holland, A. P. (Tony) Conway, Charles M. Sadusk, Virgil E. Conway and Miss Bettie Sprewls.
